claims.text: Minor compositional segregation occurs during solidification of as-cast HfNbTaTiZr.
The segregated regions have spatially different thermal expansion coefficients.
Differential thermal expansion between segregated regions generates localized internal residual stresses during thermal cycling or elevated-temperature operation.
The internal thermal stresses alter dislocation activation and mobility.
The internal thermal stresses alter microstructural evolution and phase stability over time.
Thermal-expansion-mismatch stresses enhance tensile creep in conventionally processed HfNbTaTiZr.
Thermal-expansion-mismatch stresses contribute to microhardness changes during cold rolling.
Thermal-expansion-mismatch stresses cause nonuniform or nonlinear temperature dependence of the elastic modulus.
The coupling between thermal stresses and microstructural evolution explains aging-induced hardening at 600–800 °C.
A rigorous homogenization anneal will reduce compositional segregation relative to conventional processing.
Reducing segregation through homogenization will reduce thermal-expansion mismatch and the associated internal stress fields.
Homogenized samples will have significantly lower tensile creep rates at 1250 °C than conventionally processed samples.
Homogenized samples will show less pronounced microhardness changes during cold rolling than conventionally processed samples.
Homogenized samples will exhibit a more uniform elastic modulus from 293 to 1100 K than conventionally processed samples.
Conventionally processed HfNbTaTiZr exhibits reported anomalies in creep, hardness, and elastic modulus.
The proposed thermal-expansion-mismatch mechanism operates primarily from 600 to 1250 °C.
Below 600 °C, the effect of thermal-expansion mismatch should be minimal.
The effect of thermal-expansion mismatch should be minimal when complete chemical homogeneity is achieved.
Grain size and precipitate distribution may also influence the observed behavior.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that testing is performed over 600–1250 °C, but the proposed comparison also includes room-temperature cold rolling and elastic-modulus measurements extending down to 293 K, both below 600 °C.

The boundary says the mismatch effect is minimal below 600 °C, while the hypothesis attributes room-temperature cold-rolling hardness changes to that effect and predicts that homogenization will alter those changes. No persistence of high-temperature residual stresses into the room-temperature test is explicitly specified to reconcile these statements.
